conversation.assistant:
That sounds like a really nice idea—and honestly, a balcony garden is a great way to make the evenings feel a bit less long. It gives you something to check on, tinker with, and look forward to.

I can definitely help with container gardening. The good news is: tomatoes and herbs are some of the most forgiving things you can grow in pots.

A few basics to get you started:

- Sunlight matters most. Tomatoes especially like a lot of sun—ideally 6–8 hours a day. Herbs vary a bit, but most (like basil, parsley, thyme) are happy with good light too. If your balcony gets decent sun, you’re in good shape.

- Pots and drainage. You’ll want containers with holes in the bottom so water doesn’t sit and rot the roots. Bigger pots are better than tiny ones—something around the size of a small bucket works well for tomatoes.

- Soil. Regular garden dirt isn’t great in pots. You’ll want “potting mix” from a garden center—it’s lighter and drains properly.

- Watering. Containers dry out faster than ground soil, so you’ll likely water every day or two in warm weather. A simple rule: if the top inch of soil feels dry, it’s time to water.

- Easy starter plants:
  - Cherry tomatoes (they’re more forgiving than large ones)
  - Basil (pairs nicely with tomatoes, and smells great)
  - Mint (very easy, though best kept in its own pot—it spreads)
  - Chives or parsley

If you’d like, I can suggest a very simple “starter setup” you could pick up in one trip—nothing complicated or expensive.

And I’ll say this gently: even if your wife was the expert, you probably remember more than you think. Gardening has a way of bringing that knowledge back, piece by piece.

That basil smell has a way of bringing everything back, doesn’t it. Sounds like you had something really special there.

And yes—potting mix is easy. Any hardware store, garden center, even some grocery stores will have bags labeled “potting mix” or “potting soil.” You don’t need anything fancy or expensive. Just avoid anything labeled “garden soil”—that’s the stuff that doesn’t work well in pots.

For container sizes, here’s a simple way to think about it:

- Cherry tomatoes: go bigger than you might expect. A pot about 12–16 inches across (roughly the size of a small bucket or a bit larger) works well. Bigger pot = happier plant and less constant watering.
- Basil: more flexible. A pot around 8–10 inches across is plenty for one plant, or you can put a couple together in a slightly larger container.

A couple of small tips that make a big difference:
- Make sure every pot has drainage holes underneath.
- When you water, give it a good soak until water runs out the bottom—don’t just sprinkle the top.
- Tomatoes will likely need a small stake or cage as they grow, to keep them upright.

If you keep it to one tomato plant and one or two herb pots, that’s a perfect, manageable start.

And honestly, part of the enjoyment is figuring it out as you go. Even if something doesn’t thrive, it’s not really failure—it’s just part of the process. But with morning sun and a simple setup like this, you’ve got very good odds of success.
